lines.say: Every October, something strange happens on the streets of La Porte, Indiana.
Children dressed as ghosts and witches knock on the doors of strangers and demand candy. And the strangers hand it over.
In 1866, a Philadelphia newspaper described the same night a little differently. The boys of the city, it said, were hanging dead cats to door-bells.
lines.tts: In eighteen sixty-six, a Philadelphia newspaper described the same night a little differently. The boys of the city, it said, were hanging dead cats to door-bells.

lines.say: The holiday you know is about a hundred years old. The one underneath it is much, much older. And almost everything you've been told about where it came from is wrong.
There was no Celtic god of the dead named Samhain. The church did not steal the date. The jack-o'-lantern was a turnip. And trick-or-treat began as a threat.

We'll also tell you what Halloween looked like right here, in La Porte County, over a hundred and fifty years, through the newspapers of the towns around us, and the weather records of the nights themselves.
This is the real history of Halloween: what's documented, what's legend, and what no one can prove.
Start with the part nobody puts on a greeting card. In America, Halloween was a night of vandalism long before it was a night of candy.
In 1872, Godey's Lady's Book, the biggest women's magazine in the country, complained about gangs of boys who, in its words, batter down panels, dislocate bell-wires, and unhinge gates.
lines.tts: In eighteen seventy-two, Godey's Lady's Book, the biggest women's magazine in the country, complained about gangs of boys who, in its words, batter down panels, dislocate bell-wires, and unhinge gates.

lines.say: That same fall, a paper in Terre Haute, Indiana, reported gates lifted off their hinges, door-bells pulled, and a washtub full of potatoes left in the middle of Main Street.
By the 1890s and 1900s, the papers printed the same story every November first. Gates gone. Wagons on roofs. Outhouses tipped. Windows soaped.
lines.tts: By the eighteen nineties and nineteen hundreds, the papers printed the same story every November first. Gates gone. Wagons on roofs. Outhouses tipped. Windows soaped.

lines.say: Some towns called it Cabbage Night, Gate Night, or Mischief Night. In Indianapolis, in 1891, the paper gave the night before Halloween its own name: door-bell night.
lines.tts: Some towns called it Cabbage Night, Gate Night, or Mischief Night. In Indianapolis, in eighteen ninety-one, the paper gave the night before Halloween its own name: door-bell night.

lines.say: So here is the question this film is really about. How did a night of broken gates become a night when strangers give your children chocolate?
To answer that, we have to go back about twelve hundred years, to a monastery in Ireland.
You have probably heard that Halloween comes from Samhain, an ancient Celtic festival of the dead, when the veil between the worlds grew thin.
Here is what the records actually say. The word Samhain, the first of November, appears in Irish writing from about the ninth century on.

Those writings were made by Christian monks, copying stories that were already old. In them, Samhain is the start of winter, and the night when kings held their assemblies, and when strange things happen in the tales.

Archaeologists have dug at the Hill of Ward, in County Meath, where a later legend put the great Samhain fire. They found layer on layer of burnt ground and feasting bones, going back about three thousand years.
Was that Samhain? The lead archaeologist's own words were: tempting, but difficult to conclusively prove.
Now the parts that aren't true. Samhain, the Celtic god of the dead.

No such god appears in any Irish text. He was invented in 1786 by a British army officer named Charles Vallancey, who wrote that the Irish deity Saman was the judge of departed souls. Vallancey, a reviewer said, wrote more nonsense than any man of his time.
lines.tts: No such god appears in any Irish text. He was invented in seventeen eighty-six by a British army officer named Charles Vallancey, who wrote that the Irish deity Saman was the judge of departed souls. Vallancey, a reviewer said, wrote more nonsense than any man of his time.

lines.say: The Celtic New Year. That one comes from two Victorian scholars, John Rhys and James Frazer, in the 1890s. The historian Ronald Hutton checked the medieval records. There is no record of such a festival.
lines.tts: The Celtic New Year. That one comes from two Victorian scholars, John Rhys and James Frazer, in the eighteen nineties. The historian Ronald Hutton checked the medieval records. There is no record of such a festival.

lines.say: Druids and human sacrifice at Samhain. There is no contemporary record of any pagan Samhain rite at all. Not one.

And the veil between the worlds? That phrase is modern. The old tales do have the dead and the otherworld close at Samhain. But as a line about thin veils, it's the stuff of the last hundred years, not the first thousand.
So: a real festival, at the start of winter, with real fires and real stories. A god, a new year, and a sacrifice that were added much later. That's Samhain.
The next thing everyone knows: the church moved All Saints' Day to the first of November to stamp out Samhain. Halloween is just All Hallows' Eve, the night before.
The first half is true. Hallow means saint. Hallows' Eve is the evening before All Saints. Shorten it, and you get Halloween, a word the dictionaries date to about 1700.
lines.tts: The first half is true. Hallow means saint. Hallows' Eve is the evening before All Saints. Shorten it, and you get Halloween, a word the dictionaries date to about seventeen hundred.

lines.say: The second half is where it gets interesting. Rome's first feast of all the martyrs was in May. In the year 609, Pope Boniface the Fourth dedicated the Pantheon to Mary and the martyrs, on May thirteenth.

The November date shows up in England and Germany first. By about the year 800, Charlemagne's favorite churchman, Alcuin, was keeping All Saints on the first of November. In 835, the emperor Louis the Pious made it official across his empire.
Now here's the problem for the stamp-out-Samhain theory. We can check what the Irish church itself did. And its calendars show the Irish keeping All Saints on April twentieth.
In other words, the one Celtic church we can look at wasn't using November first at all. The date came out of England and the Frankish empire, and Rome adopted it.
Was it chosen to compete with a pagan festival? Some historians say yes. Hutton says the evidence points the other way. Nobody can prove it either way.
The second of November, All Souls' Day, for everyone who had died, was added around the year 998 by an abbot in France. Now the church had two days for the dead, back to back, at the start of winter.

And that's when the door-knocking starts. In England, from at least 1511, the poor went house to house on All Hallows asking for soul cakes, small spiced cakes, in return for prayers for the family's dead.
lines.tts: And that's when the door-knocking starts. In England, from at least fifteen eleven, the poor went house to house on All Hallows asking for soul cakes, small spiced cakes, in return for prayers for the family's dead.

lines.say: Shakespeare knew it. In 1593, one of his characters is told he's puling like a beggar at Hallowmas.

lines.say: Souling. Children, at the door, asking for a treat. Four hundred years before anyone said trick or treat.
In 1785, a Scottish farmer named Robert Burns wrote a poem called Halloween. It's our best picture of what the night was like for ordinary people.
lines.tts: In seventeen eighty-five, a Scottish farmer named Robert Burns wrote a poem called Halloween. It's our best picture of what the night was like for ordinary people.

lines.say: Some merry, friendly, country folks, together did convene, to burn their nits, and pull their stocks, and hold their Halloween.
Burns added footnotes. Young people went out in the dark, hand in hand, eyes shut, and pulled up the first kale stalk they touched. Its shape told them the shape of their future husband or wife.

They named two nuts for a boy and a girl and set them in the fire, to see if they burned together or jumped apart. A girl took a candle, alone, to a mirror, and ate an apple, to see a face appear behind her.

Halloween, in 1785, was a night for finding out who you'd marry. In 1833, the painter Daniel Maclise showed the same games at a party near Blarney, in Ireland: bobbing for apples, snapping at an apple on a string.

lines.say: Now, the lantern. In Ireland and Scotland, people hollowed out turnips, carved faces in them, and put a candle inside. This one is from Ireland.
A print from the 1790s shows travelers terrified by one: The Affrightened Travellers, or, the Illuminated Turnip.

lines.say: The name jack-o'-lantern is older than the carving. In the 1600s, it meant a will-o'-the-wisp, a ghost light over a bog, and then a night watchman, a man with a lantern.

So what was Halloween like here? There's a catch. La Porte's own newspapers from those years aren't online. The Argus and the Herald sit on microfilm at the library on Indiana Avenue.
The library's own hundred-years-ago column, from the Argus of October 1922, has nothing about Halloween at all. The big news on the thirty-first was an Elks' show at the Central theatre.

lines.say: So why did it survive? Because it kept changing. A winter fire became a church feast. A church feast became a night for finding out who you'd marry. That became a night for breaking gates, and that became a deal: treat us, and we'll leave your gate alone.
And every generation told itself the night was ancient, because that made it feel like it belonged to them. Maybe that's the real tradition. Not the turnip, or the pumpkin, or the candy. The story.

Tell us yours. What did Halloween look like in La Porte when you were a kid? Which street gave out full-size candy bars? Put it in the comments. We read every one, and the best ones go in the next film.
